definition: Mechanical facilities spaced along a pipeline that create the pressure differentials needed to push gas forward, functioning like a heart pumping blood through the network.
core_idea: A compressor station works like a household fan: it draws gas in on a low-pressure side and discharges it on a high-pressure side, and chaining many such stations together in series keeps gas flowing continuously down the pipeline.
key_points: Simple mental model: a fan pulls gas in (low pressure zone) on one side and pushes it out (high pressure zone) on the other
Stations are typically spaced roughly every 50 miles along a pipeline
A modern station usually runs several compressor units in parallel
Gas path through a station: suction header, then a scrubber system, then compression/cooling stages, then discharge into the next pipeline segment
Gas moves between segments by flowing from one station's high-pressure discharge to the next station's low-pressure suction
All stations on a pipeline must operate in coordination or the whole pipeline stops working; most are automated and coordinated by a central computer
relationships: Depends on the continuous injection/withdrawal requirement
Cooling stages tie into compression heating/corrosion effects
trading_implications: Physical pipeline capacity is not a single uniform pipe but a chain of segments bounded by compressor stations, which is relevant to understanding where physical constraints or outages could occur
caveats: Thinking of a pipeline as one continuous unregulated pipe rather than a series of pressure-managed segments
